stimulus.text:
Saint-Domingue (the French colony on the western part of Hispaniola), about 1791:

| Group | Number |
|---|---|
| Enslaved Africans | about 500,000 |
| Free whites | about 30,000 |
| Free people of mixed race (gens de couleur) | about 30,000 |

Free people of mixed race owned about a third of the enslaved people on the island but were barred from political participation.
stimulus.source_note: Figures as given in Barron's AP U.S. History Premium, 2027, Chapter 5, Topic 3.6.

books.section: Topic 3.6 The Influence of Revolutionary Ideals, C. The Impact of the American Revolution Abroad

stem: News of the slave rebellion in Saint-Domingue most directly alarmed planters in the southern United States because it showed that

options.text: France would invade the southern states to free enslaved people
options.misconception: France never planned such an invasion; the fear was of rebellion at home, not of a French army landing in the South.

options.text: Enslaved people could overthrow a slave society and win independence for themselves
The United States would have to send troops to defend France
options.misconception: The United States sent no troops to Saint-Domingue; Washington's government stayed neutral in the French wars.

options.text: Sugar planting would collapse and ruin the American economy
options.misconception: Sugar was Saint-Domingue's crop, not the American South's; the alarm was about rebellion spreading, not about sugar prices.

rationales.B: Saint-Domingue's enslaved people rose, defeated their owners, and built Haiti, the first Black republic. Background: fleeing whites and free people of color carried stories of the rebellion to southern ports.
rationales.A: No French invasion threatened the South; the planters feared their own enslaved workers, inspired by the example.
rationales.C: America sent no troops; neutrality kept the United States out of France's wars entirely.
rationales.D: Sugar prices were not the fear; the fear was that enslaved people at home would do what Saint-Domingue's had done.
rationales.general:
1. Read the numbers. A slave society where the enslaved outnumbered the free eight to one.
2. Ask what happened. Background: the enslaved rose and won their freedom, building Haiti by 1804.
3. Ask who listened. Background: southern planters held people in the same conditions and feared the same rising.
Remember: an example alarms those who live the same way — ask who shares the conditions, not who shares the border.
